title: Catherine the Dominican
hook: Catherine of Siena lived as a Dominican laywoman, at home, in a black cloak

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rosary story: a tradition about Dominic, and a prayer that grew from many hands. Your line was a story that grew. What did you find in your life that many hands built? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-eight.

Siena, in Italy. A dyer's house, loud with family, the smell of the vats drifting in from the work yard. One of the daughters will not marry. Her family pushes; she refuses. She doesn't run off to a convent, either. Instead she asks to join a group of local women who wear a white dress and a black cloak, and who live in their own homes. For a while she barely leaves a small room in her parents' house. Then she walks out of it, and she doesn't stop: sickrooms, prisons, city councils, and eventually the pope's court. Her name was Catherine. Today, the woman in the black cloak.
screen: `SIENA, A DYER'S HOUSE.` → `SHE WON'T MARRY. NO CONVENT, EITHER.` → `A WHITE DRESS, A BLACK CLOAK.`

segments.voice: The women were called the mantellate, from the Italian for a mantle, a cloak. They belonged to the Dominican family as laywomen, doing penance and works of mercy, not as cloistered nuns. Catherine became one, a mantellata, and that changes how to picture her. She wasn't behind convent walls. She lived at home and went out into the city. Her confessor, the Dominican Raymond of Capua, wrote her life, and he tells of her nursing the sick and visiting prisoners. In one of her own letters she describes sitting with a young man condemned to death, staying with him to the end. Matthew's Gospel names that kind of love. In the Douay-Rheims: "I was sick, and you visited me: I was in prison, and you came to me." Then came the letters. Catherine dictated letters to kings, to city leaders, to cardinals, and to the pope himself, who was living in Avignon, in France, far from Rome. She wrote to him plainly, with respect and with fire, urging him to come back to Rome and to make peace. Her thinking about God and the soul, gathered in a book called the Dialogue, is still read, and the Church calls her a Doctor of the Church, a teacher for everyone. All of it from a laywoman in a cloak, living in her parents' house. Being a Dominican, she showed, isn't only for friars and nuns. It's a family with room at the kitchen table.
screen: `THE MANTELLATE: A CLOAK, NOT A CLOISTER.` · `THE SICK, THE PRISONERS, THE CONDEMNED.` · `LETTERS TO THE POPE IN AVIGNON.` · `A DOCTOR OF THE CHURCH, FROM HOME.` · then, large: `I WAS SICK, AND YOU VISITED ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for Dominican laity, and for all the Catherines in ordinary clothes. Settle, and breathe. Today there are still lay Dominicans: people with jobs and families who belong to the Dominican family and pray its prayers. Bring them to mind, though you may never meet one. Then widen the circle. Bring to mind someone you know who lives their faith without a habit or a title: the neighbor who drives people to chemo, the aunt who visits the nursing home. Hold them for a few breaths. If you pray, you can ask Saint Catherine to pray for them. If not, simply thank them silently, one by one. The bell holds the time.
Catherine the Dominican. Catherine of Siena, a mantellata: a Dominican laywoman in a black cloak who nursed, wrote and counseled popes from home. Today's word.
Your line: the mantellata. Today, put on your ordinary clothes like a cloak with a purpose: visit, call or write to one person who is sick or shut in. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Lay Dominicans belong to fraternities attached to the Order of Preachers, making a promise, meeting to pray and study, and serving in ordinary life; Catholics honor Catherine of Siena as a Doctor of the Church and read her Dialogue and letters.

notes: Claims rule: no dates, birth order or family size (she is traditionally the 24th or 23rd child), and no year of the Doctor title (1970) or patronages. Confirm 'a dyer's house' (her father Giacomo Benincasa was a wool dyer).
Confirm the description of the Mantellate as Dominican laywomen of penance living at home (later the Dominican Third Order), with white habit and black mantle.
The condemned young man is Niccolò di Toldo, from her letter to Raymond of Capua; described without name. Confirm.
Confirm the summary that she urged Gregory XI to return from Avignon to Rome and to make peace; no claim that she caused the return.
'the Church calls her a Doctor of the Church, a teacher for everyone' — confirm the gloss.
'the smell of the vats drifting in from the work yard' is scene-setting, not a sourced claim; cut if a Keeper prefers.
Douay-Rheims wording of Matthew 25:36 to confirm.
